claim: A total of 57,193 cells were included for single-cell sequencing analysis from human skeletal muscle biopsy.
source: A total of 57,193 cells were included for analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cells analyzed in the single-cell sequencing experiment.

claim: The cells from human skeletal muscle were grouped into nine cell populations.
source: The cells were grouped to nine cell populations (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1a and b which shows the UMAP plot with cell clusters.

claim: Myogenic progenitors accounted for 12.4% of all the mononuclear cells from human skeletal muscle.
source: Especially, myogenic progenitors accounted for 12.4% of all the mononuclear cells, while tenocytes only accounted for 0.06% (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from the single-cell sequencing data analysis.

claim: Tenocytes accounted for only 0.06% of all mononuclear cells from human skeletal muscle.
source: Especially, myogenic progenitors accounted for 12.4% of all the mononuclear cells, while tenocytes only accounted for 0.06% (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from the single-cell sequencing data analysis.

claim: All CD29+/CD56+ cells identified in the scRNA-seq data were myogenic progenitors.
source: The scRNA-seq data revealed that all the CD29+/CD56+ cells were myogenic progenitors, which occupied 19.3% of all the myogenic progenitors (Figure 1e).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from joint expression analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: CD29+/CD56+ cells occupied 19.3% of all myogenic progenitors.
source: The scRNA-seq data revealed that all the CD29+/CD56+ cells were myogenic progenitors, which occupied 19.3% of all the myogenic progenitors (Figure 1e).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentage from the single-cell sequencing data analysis.

claim: There were no tenocytes with CD29+/CD56+ expression in the scRNA-seq data.
source: However, there existed no tenocytes with CD29+/CD56+ (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from joint expression analysis.

claim: Nearly all isolated CD29+/CD56+ cells were positively stained with PAX7, MYOD1, and MYF5 myogenic progenitor markers.
source: The collected cells were stained with anti-PAX7, anti-MYOD1, and anti-MYF5 antibody to confirm the purity of isolated CD29+/CD56+ cells, and nearly all of the obtained cells were positively stained with these myogenic progenitors markers (Figure 1f and g).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence staining results confirming the identity of isolated cells.

claim: Human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors have high in vitro expansion ability.
source: The proliferation assay indicated high in vitro expansion ability of these human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors (Figure 1h).
evidence: The manuscript describes proliferation assay results showing cell expansion over time.

claim: Approximately 90% of nuclei were present in MyHC-positive myotubes after differentiation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: Approximately 90% of nuclei were present in myosin heavy chain (MyHC)-positive myotubes (Figure 1i and j).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification of myogenic differentiation efficiency from immunofluorescence staining.

claim: The expression of PAX7, MYF5, and MYOD1 decreased after myogenic differentiation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: Consistently, the expression of PAX7, MYF5, and MYOD1 was enriched in the myogenic progenitors, and their expression decreased after differentiation as shown by RT-qPCR assays (Figure 1k).
evidence: The manuscript describes RT-qPCR results showing gene expression changes during differentiation.

claim: The expression of MYOG, MYH1, and MYH3 was significantly upregulated in differentiated myotubes from human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: In contrast, the expression of genes marking differentiation such as myogenin (MYOG), myosin heavy chain 1 (MYH1), and myosin heavy chain 3 (MYH3) was significantly upregulated in differentiated myotubes (Figure 1l).
evidence: The manuscript describes RT-qPCR results showing upregulation of differentiation markers.

claim: The expression of tendon markers TNC and SCX was significantly increased after tenogenic differentiation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: Furthermore, the expression of tendon markers such as TNC and SCX was significantly increased (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence and RT-qPCR results showing increased expression of tendon markers.

claim: Tendon-related genes COL I, MKX, THBS4, and COMP were enriched after tendon differentiation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: Moreover, some other tendon-related genes, such as COL I, MKX, THBS4, and COMP, were also enriched after tendon differentiation (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript describes RT-qPCR results showing enrichment of tendon-related genes.

claim: Only about 20% of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors showed MYOG and MyHC expression after 12 days of tenogenic induction.
source: Compared to the over 90% of differentiation efficiency upon myogenic differentiation, only about 20% of cells showed MYOG and MyHC expression after 12 days of tenogenic induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification comparing myogenic marker expression during tenogenic differentiation.

claim: Approximately 40% of CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors displayed tenogenic differentiation ability in clonal analysis.
source: Approximately 40% of CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors displayed tenogenic differentiation ability (Figure 2g), suggesting that human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors have tenogenic differentiation potential.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification from clonal differentiation assays.

claim: Over 95% of wells with alive cells showed MyHC+ myotubes in clonal myogenic differentiation assays.
source: MyHC+ myotubes were observed in over 95% of wells with alive cells (Figure 2g).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification from clonal differentiation assays.

claim: Tenocytes differentiated from human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors share high similarity to fresh isolated tenocytes from human tendons.
source: The differentiated tendon cells share high similarity to fresh isolated tenocytes from human tendons (Figure 3a), suggesting that human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors are capable of tendon differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript describes RNA sequencing analysis comparing expression profiles.

claim: Terms related to skeletal muscle functions were enriched upon skeletal muscle differentiation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: Upon the skeletal muscle differentiation, terms related to skeletal muscle functions such as skeletal muscle thin filament assembly, skeletal muscle contraction, muscle organ development, and sarcomere organization were enriched (Figure 3d), suggesting the muscular identity of the differentiated cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes GO analysis results of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Terms related to tendon formation, tendon development, and tendon cell differentiation were enriched after tenogenic differentiation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: In contrast, terms related to tendon formation, tendon development, and tendon cell differentiation were enriched after tenogenic differentiation (Figure 3e), suggesting that tendon identity is achieved in the differentiated cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes GO analysis results of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Murine MuSCs failed to be induced to tendon cells upon the same induction condition as that for human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: In sharp contrast to human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors, murine MuSCs failed to be induced to tendon cells upon the same induction condition as that for human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors, though the myogenic differentiation is as efficient as the human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results comparing mouse and human cells under identical conditions.

claim: 93.9% of nuclei were present in MyHC+ myotubes after myogenic differentiation of murine MuSCs.
source: After myogenic differentiation, 93.9% of nuclei were present in MyHC+ myotubes (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification of myogenic differentiation efficiency for mouse MuSCs.

claim: No Scx+ cells were observed after 12 days of tenogenic differentiation induction for murine MuSCs.
source: In sharp contrast, no Scx+ cells were observed after 12 days of induction for tenogenic differentiation (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence staining results showing absence of tendon marker.

claim: The expression of tendon-related genes Scx, Tnc, Col I, Mkx, and Thbs4 did not increase after tenogenic differentiation of murine MuSCs.
source: Different from human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors, the expression of genes indicating tendon cell fate such as Scx, Tnc, Col I, Mkx, and Thbs4 did not increase after tenogenic differentiation (Figure 4d), suggesting the failure to induce tenogenic cell fate from murine MuSCs.
evidence: The manuscript describes RT-qPCR results showing no increase in tendon marker expression.

claim: Less than 0.2% tendon cells originated from mouse MuSCs were observed even 4 months after tendon removal in lineage tracing experiments.
source: Nevertheless, less than 0.2% tendon cells originated from mouse MuSCs were observed even 4 months after tendon removal (Figure 4f–g).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification from lineage tracing experiments in mice.

claim: Over 75% of transplanted human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors showed TNC expression in vivo.
source: Immunofluorescence staining revealed that over 75% of the human cells showed TNC expression (Figure 5b and d), suggesting that the majority of the transplanted human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors differentiate to tendon cells in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification from immunofluorescence analysis of transplanted cells.

claim: Only about 12.8% of transplanted human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors expressed MyHC in vivo.
source: Only about 12.8% of the human cells detected expressed MyHC (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification from immunofluorescence analysis of transplanted cells.

claim: The majority (80.0% and 74.6%) of transplanted human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors expressed SCX and TNMD.
source: The majority (80.0% and 74.6%) of transplanted human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors also expressed SCX and TNMD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, b and c).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification from immunofluorescence analysis of transplanted cells.

claim: Col I was predominantly expressed in the regenerated tendon-like tissue rather than Col III after human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitor transplantation.
source: Furthermore, Col I was predominantly expressed in the regenerated tendon-like tissue rather than Col III after human cells transplantation (Figure 5e), indicating human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors could contribute to structural repair of injured tendon and facilitate the healing process.
evidence: The manuscript describes immunofluorescence staining results showing differential collagen expression.

claim: Less than 0.3% of tdTomato+TNC+ cells were detected when murine MuSCs were transplanted to pre-injured tendon.
source: In sharp contrast to human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors, when 50,000 murine MuSCs constitutively expressing tdTomato were transplanted to pre-injured tendon in NOD/SCID mice under the same condition, less than 0.3% of tdTomato+TNC+ cells were detected (Figure 5f and g).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantification from immunofluorescence analysis of transplanted mouse cells.

claim: Transplantation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors resulted in larger and denser collagen fibrils compared to PBS injection control.
source: Larger and denser collagen fibrils of the tendons were identified in the transplanted group than the control group with PBS injection, although the maturation level of collagen fibrils could still not reach those in the uninjured tendon (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: The manuscript describes TEM analysis results comparing collagen fibril structure.

claim: The max failure load and stiffness of tendons from the transplantation group were significantly better than those from the PBS injection control group.
source: The max failure load and stiffness of the tendons from the transplantation group were significantly better than those from the PBS injection control group (Figure 6c).
evidence: The manuscript describes biomechanical testing results comparing transplanted and control groups.

claim: Transplantation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors contributed to improving both twitch and tetanus plantarflexion force compared to PBS injection control.
source: Expectedly, transplantation of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors for the injured tendon also contributed to improving both twitch and tetanus plantarflexion force when compared with the PBS injection control group, although the plantarflexion force could still not reach the level of the uninjured leg (Figure 6d).
evidence: The manuscript describes functional testing results comparing transplanted and control groups.

claim: The endurance time and max fatigue speed of mice transplanted with human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors were better in treadmill test compared to PBS group.
source: Consistent with the improved plantarflexion force, the endurance time and max fatigue speed of the mice transplanted with human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors were better in treadmill test when compared to the PBS group (Figure 6e).
evidence: The manuscript describes treadmill testing results comparing transplanted and control groups.

claim: TGFβ signaling was identified in KEGG enrichment analysis of upregulated genes in human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors when compared with murine MuSCs.
source: Interestingly, TGFβ signaling was identified in KEGG enrichment analysis of upregulated genes in human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors when compared with murine MuSCs (Figure 7a), indicating that TGFβ signaling could be the key node for maintaining the tendon differentiation potential.
evidence: The manuscript describes KEGG pathway analysis results from RNA sequencing data comparison.

claim: SMAD2 and SMAD3 were identified in upregulated gene set enriched in TGFβ signaling pathway in human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors.
source: Especially, SMAD2 and SMAD3 were identified in upregulated gene set which was enriched in TGFβ signaling pathway (Figure 7b).
evidence: The manuscript describes specific genes identified in pathway analysis.

claim: TGFβ signaling inhibitor SB-431542 significantly suppressed expression level of tendon-related genes SCX, TNC, COL I, MKX, and THBS4.
source: The immunofluorescent staining, western blot assay, and RT-qPCR results showed SB-431542 significantly suppressed expression level of tendon-related genes SCX, TNC, COL I, MKX, and THBS4 (Figure 7c–e).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results using TGFβ signaling inhibitor.

claim: Myogenic differentiation ability of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors was increased after treatment of SB-431542 during tenogenic induction.
source: On the contrary, myogenic differentiation ability of human CD29+/CD56+ myogenic progenitors was increased after treatment of SB-431542 during tenogenic induction (Figure 7f and g).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results showing increased myogenic differentiation with TGFβ inhibitor.

claim: MuSCs are adult stem cells located at the periphery of myofibers between the basal lamina and the plasmalemma.
source: MuSCs are adult stem cells located at the periphery of myofibers between the basal lamina and the plasmalemma of the myofibers and responsible for muscle regeneration (Fu et al., 2015a; Relaix et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature to establish background knowledge about MuSCs.

claim: MuSCs are responsible for muscle regeneration.

evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature to establish background knowledge about MuSCs.

source: The CD56+CD34+ progenitor cells isolated from human skeletal muscle biopsies have been reported to have chondrogenic, adipogenic, and osteogenic potentials besides myogenic potential (Zheng et al., 2007; Castiglioni et al., 2014; Pisani et al., 2010a).
